en.title: Former OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy proposed the "LLM Wiki" concept on GitHub in April, arguing that unstructured documents should be compiled into a reasoning-ready knowledge network to address the inefficiency of repeated retrieval and reasoning in large models.

en.title:
Looks like Seedance is about to get steamrolled — MAGI-2-preview now runs on 96GB of VRAM. The community's NVFP4 quant version:
· Compresses only the expert weights, shrinking the transformer from 228GB to 71.8GB
· 96GB VRAM plus 64GB RAM, with the entire model loaded into VRAM and no offload support
· 4-bit only saves VRAM and load time (60.5s → 9.5s); per-step speed is essentially unchanged
· In ComfyUI, install the author's node pack and use the built-in Load…
en.reason: Community NVFP4 quantization cuts MAGI-2-preview's transformer from 228GB to 71.8GB, letting 96GB VRAM plus 64GB RAM hold it without offload and load in 9.5s instead of 60.5s, though a 10s 540p 100-step run still takes 32m47s on RTX PRO 6000.

en.title:
Breaking the capability ceiling: a methodology of ambition and cognition for the AI era

01 In business, there is a widely held view: a founder's ceiling is often set by the ceiling of their ambition and cognition.

en.title: Agent Context Management and Observability Design
en.summary:
Agent Context Management and Observability Design

The current codebase **already borrows** some of smolagents' context and observability design:
*   Step-based memory via `AgentMemory` / `TaskStep` / `ActionStep`;
*   `Timing`, `TokenUsage`, and `[META]` statistics;
*   LangChain callback metrics for ReAct.
1.   **Context budget for a single Agent run**: previously every step replayed the full history, so long tasks grew without bound;
2.   **Structured observability logs**: previously there were `[META]` and plain logs, but no stable JSON events, making it impossible to trace a run by step / LLM / tool.
├─ Session level: chat_summaries + recent messages (existing)
├─ Run level: keep the most recent N ActionSteps + a character budget (new)

en.reason: Borrowing smolagents’ step memory and [META] timing/token stats, the design adds a run-level MULTISTEP_CONTEXT_MAX_CHARS=32000 budget, keeps the latest 8 ActionSteps, caps each Observation at 6000 characters, and emits agent.trace JSON events for step, LLM, and tool tracking.

en.title: Has Spring AI Alibaba really stopped getting updates? I scoured its GitHub top to bottom
en.summary:
Spring AI Alibaba Has Really Stopped Updating? I Dug Through Its Entire GitHub

The Juejin trending post "Spring AI Alibaba Has Stopped Updating — Does Java Still Have Hope?" is still on the leaderboard today, with 16k in heat and 94 comments. Its argument is simple: the last official release is still v1.1.2.2, published on March 10 this year. I'm inclined to believe the conclusion, but the evidence doesn't quite satisfy me. For a repo with 11k stars backed by Alibaba, is a single number on the Releases page enough to conclude that it has "stopped updating"? How much information in between gets missed? As it happens, I have an old project using SAA, stuck at 1.1.x, and whether I upgrade depends entirely on whether the project still has momentum. So I spent half an hour going through its GitHub, from Releases to the commit log to the issue panel. The conclusion is more interesting than the rumor: the "stopped updating" claim is half right, but the other half it misses is more worth pondering than the words "stopped updating."

curl -s "https://api.github.com/repos/alibab

en.title: If all AI tools vanished tomorrow, what should individuals and teams really hold onto?
en.summary:
Title: If All AI Tools Disappeared Tomorrow, What Should Individuals and Teams Really Keep?

A while back I came across an article titled "After AI Tools Exit: What R&D Teams Should Really Keep." The author was a R&D team leader. Although I left the workplace two years ago, I read it in one sitting—it's full of insights that are highly illuminating for those still working.

What struck me most was its angle. Over the past two years, everyone has been talking about what else AI can do, but this article flips the question: **if all AI tools vanished, what would teams still have left?** Its focus is on teams.

I previously wrote a piece: "**AI Can Do Everything You Can—Why Does the Company Still Need You?**" That was a question for individuals.

I think this topic is very meaningful, so this time I'm putting individuals and teams together.

It's worth sharing, so today we won't talk tech or tools—we'll talk about: "**If all AI tools disappeared tomorrow, what should individuals and teams really keep?**"

Over the past two years, AI has advanced with unstoppable momentum—far too fast. Writing code, reading documents, building Agents, making videos, operating web pages, controlling computers—AI has learned one thing after another.

> **"In the AI era, as long as you learn slowly enough, you don't have to learn."**

en.title: Google is at it again: Gemini can now be used in Claude Code/Codex, and it goes hard.
en.summary:
Google's at it again: Gemini can now pull its weight inside Claude Code/Codex

Gemini 4 Neon's capabilities are no longer in doubt—even the Antigravity app has become genuinely usable lately. And beyond that, Antigravity skins are starting to take off, even though the official app doesn't support them yet.

Of course, if you're already used to Claude Code, Codex or Pi and don't want to use Antigravity but still want Gemini 4 Neon, you can hook it up through gemini-api. It bundles models like Gemini 4 Neon, image generation and voice, long-document parsing and cloud-hosted Agents into a single-file command that you drop into your system path, so your existing Agent can call Gemini in for backup from the terminal whenever it likes. It works with just one API key, which you can apply for in Google's AI Studio.

en.reason: The `gemini-api-cli` v0.5.0 single-file command wires Gemini 4 Neon, image generation and TTS into Claude Code, Codex or Pi with one AI Studio API key; a free-tier test produced a 75,388-byte WAV from 39 tokens while `gemini-4-neon` and image calls returned 429.

en.title: This open-source AI browser automation framework Stagehand is seriously impressive.
en.summary:
This open-source AI browser automation framework Stagehand is seriously impressive!

Today I'm sharing an open-source project: Stagehand, an AI browser automation framework from Browserbase.

Anyone building Agents eventually hits the same problem: the Agent has to operate web pages—log into backends, fill out forms, scrape data from pages. Doing it by hand with mouse clicks is too slow, and hardcoded scripts are too brittle. Stagehand is built for exactly this.

*   From Browserbase, a company whose main business is cloud browser infrastructure; the framework is under the MIT license
*   Open-sourced in March 2024, racked up 26,000 stars in two and a half years, and the repo was still getting commits on November 14
*   TypeScript, Python, and Go SDKs maintained in the same repo; the latest npm package is 4.4.0, released November 4
*   The official tagline is twice as fast as Playwright with 80% fewer tokens—claims like these can't be verified, so take them with a grain of salt

What it does is simple, in one sentence: **a browser SDK for AI Agents, where finding elements, clicking buttons, filling forms, and extracting data are all done in natural language**
en.reason: Browserbase’s MIT-licensed Stagehand, with 26,000 GitHub stars and TypeScript, Python and Go SDKs, turns clicks, forms and data extraction into natural-language actions whose selectors replay and self-heal, using 7.4k tokens in its demo versus Playwright’s 35.7k.

en.title: Former OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy proposed the "LLM Wiki" concept on GitHub in April, arguing that unstructured documents should be compiled into a reasoning-ready knowledge network to address the inefficiency of repeated retrieval and reasoning in large models.
en.reason: Andrej Karpathy’s April GitHub LLM Wiki concept, which drew over 10,000 stars, became an enterprise product eight months later when Haimayun launched lumimax, supporting tens of millions of characters of multimodal ingestion and DEN-based cross-document knowledge graphs with conflict detection.

en.title:
Looks like Seedance is about to get steamrolled — MAGI-2-preview now runs on 96GB of VRAM. The community's NVFP4 quant version:
· Compresses only the expert weights, shrinking the transformer from 228GB to 71.8GB
· 96GB VRAM plus 64GB RAM, with the entire model loaded into VRAM and no offload support
· 4-bit only saves VRAM and load time (60.5s → 9.5s); per-step speed is essentially unchanged
· In ComfyUI, install the author's node pack and use the built-in Load…
en.reason: Community NVFP4 quantization cuts MAGI-2-preview's transformer from 228GB to 71.8GB, letting 96GB VRAM plus 64GB RAM hold it without offload and load in 9.5s instead of 60.5s, though a 10s 540p 100-step run still takes 32m47s on RTX PRO 6000.

*   Step-based memory via `AgentMemory` / `TaskStep` / `ActionStep`;

en.summary:
Spring AI Alibaba Has Really Stopped Updating? I Dug Through Its Entire GitHub

The Juejin trending post "Spring AI Alibaba Has Stopped Updating — Does Java Still Have Hope?" is still on the leaderboard today, with 16k in heat and 94 comments. Its argument is simple: the last official release is still v1.1.2.2, published on March 10 this year. I'm inclined to believe the conclusion, but the evidence doesn't quite satisfy me. For a repo with 11k stars backed by Alibaba, is a single number on the Releases page enough to conclude that it has "stopped updating"? How much information in between gets missed? As it happens, I have an old project using SAA, stuck at 1.1.x, and whether I upgrade depends entirely on whether the project still has momentum. So I spent half an hour going through its GitHub, from Releases to the commit log to the issue panel. The conclusion is more interesting than the rumor: the "stopped updating" claim is half right, but the other half it misses is more worth pondering than the words "stopped updating."

en.title: If all AI tools vanished tomorrow, what should individuals and teams really hold onto?

Title: If All AI Tools Disappeared Tomorrow, What Should Individuals and Teams Really Keep?

A while back I came across an article titled "After AI Tools Exit: What R&D Teams Should Really Keep." The author was a R&D team leader. Although I left the workplace two years ago, I read it in one sitting—it's full of insights that are highly illuminating for those still working.

What struck me most was its angle. Over the past two years, everyone has been talking about what else AI can do, but this article flips the question: **if all AI tools vanished, what would teams still have left?** Its focus is on teams.

I previously wrote a piece: "**AI Can Do Everything You Can—Why Does the Company Still Need You?**" That was a question for individuals.

I think this topic is very meaningful, so this time I'm putting individuals and teams together.

It's worth sharing, so today we won't talk tech or tools—we'll talk about: "**If all AI tools disappeared tomorrow, what should individuals and teams really keep?**"

Over the past two years, AI has advanced with unstoppable momentum—far too fast. Writing code, reading documents, building Agents, making videos, operating web pages, controlling computers—AI has learned one thing after another.

> **"In the AI era, as long as you learn slowly enough, you don't have to learn."**

en.reason: A demo that turns a requirement number into documents, test cases and business code frames the question of what individuals and teams retain if all AI tools vanish tomorrow, stressing requirements, interface contracts, domain models and data permissions.

en.title: This open-source AI browser automation framework Stagehand is seriously impressive.
en.summary:
This open-source AI browser automation framework Stagehand is seriously impressive!

Today I'm sharing an open-source project: Stagehand, an AI browser automation framework from Browserbase.

Anyone building Agents eventually hits the same problem: the Agent has to operate web pages—log into backends, fill out forms, scrape data from pages. Doing it by hand with mouse clicks is too slow, and hardcoded scripts are too brittle. Stagehand is built for exactly this.

*   From Browserbase, a company whose main business is cloud browser infrastructure; the framework is under the MIT license
*   Open-sourced in March 2024, racked up 26,000 stars in two and a half years, and the repo was still getting commits on November 14
*   TypeScript, Python, and Go SDKs maintained in the same repo; the latest npm package is 4.4.0, released November 4
*   The official tagline is twice as fast as Playwright with 80% fewer tokens—claims like these can't be verified, so take them with a grain of salt

What it does is simple, in one sentence: **a browser SDK for AI Agents, where finding elements, clicking buttons, filling forms, and extracting data are all done in natural language**
en.reason: Browserbase’s MIT-licensed Stagehand, with 26,000 GitHub stars and TypeScript, Python and Go SDKs, turns clicks, forms and data extraction into natural-language actions whose selectors replay and self-heal, using 7.4k tokens in its demo versus Playwright’s 35.7k.
